title: Rust Programming with RustRover
subtitle: Write fast, memory-safe Rust in RustRover: ownership and borrowing, enums and pattern matching, traits and generics, iterators, tests and a command-line tool.
outcomes: Explain Rust's ownership, borrowing and lifetime rules, and fix the compiler errors that enforce them
Model data with structs and enums, and handle every case with pattern matching
Handle missing values and failures with Option, Result, the ? operator and custom error types
Write reusable code with traits, generics and trait objects
Process data with collections, closures and iterator chains
Organise a Cargo package into modules, test it with unit, integration and doc tests, and ship a command-line tool
prerequisites: Confident programming in another language (functions, loops, structs or classes, and collections), as in Python Programming with PyCharm, Java Programming with IntelliJ IDEA or Go Programming with GoLand. You need Rust installed with rustup (rustup.rs), which brings cargo, rustfmt and Clippy (on Windows it also needs the Visual Studio C++ build tools), and RustRover, which is free for non-commercial use such as learning.
description:
Rust gives you the speed and control of a systems language with guarantees no other mainstream language offers: no null pointers, no use-after-free, no data races, all checked before the program runs. The price is learning to think like its compiler, and this course teaches exactly that, in RustRover, JetBrains' IDE for Rust. Every lesson teaches part of the language and shows it in RustRover step by step, with the keyboard shortcuts for macOS, Windows and Linux: running Cargo, reading and fixing compiler errors with quick-fixes, navigating the standard library, refactoring, debugging and the test runner.

You start with ownership, borrowing and lifetimes, deliberately breaking the rules to read the errors the compiler gives. Then you model data with structs, enums and pattern matching, handle failure with Option, Result and the ? operator, share behaviour with traits and generics, and process data with collections, closures and iterators. The last module organises a package into a library, a binary and modules, tests it with unit, integration and doc tests, and builds a command-line tool. Each module ends with a lab, from fixing a program the borrow checker rejects to building and testing csvsum, and the capstone is logstat, a log analyser that must match a given report exactly.

modules.title: Ownership, borrowing and lifetimes
modules.summary: Set up Rust and RustRover, then learn the rules that make Rust memory-safe without a garbage collector: ownership and moves, borrowing with shared and mutable references, and lifetimes, with the compiler errors that enforce each one.

lessons.title: Cargo, RustRover and your first program
objectives: Create, build and run a Cargo project in RustRover
Explain what Cargo.toml and the target folder hold
Use let, mut and shadowing
key_points: Rust compiles to fast native code with no garbage collector, and its compiler checks memory safety and data races before the program ever runs. rustup installs and updates the toolchain: rustc, Cargo, rustfmt and Clippy.

Cargo is Rust's build tool and package manager. cargo new hello makes a package with Cargo.toml (its name, version, edition and dependencies) and src/main.rs; cargo run builds and runs it, and cargo check only checks it, which is quicker.

Builds go in the target folder: target/debug by default, and target/release with cargo build --release, which optimises the code but takes longer. The edition, such as edition = "2024", fixes which edition of the language's rules the crate uses.
Variables are immutable unless declared with mut, as in let mut count = 1. Assigning to an immutable variable is a compile error (E0384), so every change to a value is visible in the code.
let can shadow an earlier variable with a new one of the same name, even of a different type. println! is a macro (the ! says so), and {name} inside its format string prints the variable name.

lessons.title: Ownership and moves
objectives: State Rust's ownership rules
Explain moves, copies and clones
Read and fix a use-after-move error
key_points: Every value in Rust has one owner, a variable. When the owner goes out of scope the value is dropped and its memory freed, so there's no garbage collector and no manual freeing.

A String owns its text on the heap, while a &str is a borrowed view of text, such as a string literal. Assigning a String or passing it to a function moves ownership, and the old variable can't be used any more.
Using a moved value is a compile error, E0382 borrow of moved value, so two owners can never free the same memory. The compiler's message points at the line where the move happened.
Simple values that live entirely on the stack, such as integers, floats, bool, char and tuples of them, are Copy: assigning one copies it, and both variables stay usable.
clone() makes an explicit deep copy when you really need two independent values. A function can also give ownership back by returning the value, as shout does.

lessons.title: Borrowing and references
objectives: Pass values by reference with & and &mut
Explain the borrowing rules, and how long a borrow lasts
Use slices: &[T] and &str
key_points: A reference borrows a value without taking ownership: &words is a shared reference and &mut words a mutable one. A function that only reads data takes a reference, as fn total_len(words: &[String]) does, so the caller keeps the value.

At any moment you can have either any number of shared references to a value or exactly one mutable reference, never both. This rule is what rules out data races and invalidated iterators at compile time.
A borrow lasts until the reference's last use, not to the end of its scope (non-lexical lifetimes), so code can push to a vector once an earlier shared borrow of it is no longer used.
Breaking the rule gives E0502, cannot borrow as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable. The usual fixes are to finish with the shared reference first, or to clone the data you need from it.
Slices borrow part of a collection: &v[1..3] is a &[T] and &s[0..5] a &str. Taking &str rather than &String, and &[T] rather than &Vec<T>, lets a function accept more kinds of argument.

lessons.title: Lifetimes
objectives: Explain what lifetime annotations describe
Annotate functions and structs that hold references
Apply the elision rules, and read the E0106 and E0597 errors
key_points: A lifetime is the stretch of code for which a reference is valid. The borrow checker compares lifetimes so that no reference can outlive the data it points to: E0597, does not live long enough.

Annotations such as fn longest<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str don't change how long anything lives. They tell the compiler how inputs and outputs relate: here, the result is valid only while both inputs are.

Elision rules fill in lifetimes in common cases: each reference parameter gets its own lifetime; if there's exactly one input lifetime, the outputs get it; and in a method taking &self, the outputs get self's lifetime.
When the rules can't decide, as with two reference parameters and a reference result, the compiler asks for annotations with E0106, missing lifetime specifier, and suggests where they go.

A struct that holds a reference needs a lifetime parameter, struct Excerpt<'a> { text: &'a str }, so it can't outlive what it borrows. 'static is the lifetime of data that lasts for the whole program, such as string literals.
Owning data, a String rather than a &str, needs no lifetime annotations at all, and is often the simplest choice for structs that must live a long time.

modules.title: Structs, enums and pattern matching
modules.summary: Model data with structs and their methods, with enums whose variants carry data, and with exhaustive pattern matching; then handle missing values and failures with Option, Result and the ? operator.

lessons.title: Structs and methods
objectives: Define structs, including tuple structs
Write methods and associated functions in impl blocks
Derive Debug, Clone and PartialEq, and print with {:?}
key_points: A struct names a group of fields: struct Player { name: String, score: u32 }. Create one by giving every field; Player { name, score } is shorthand when variables share the fields' names, and ..other copies the remaining fields from another value.

Methods go in an impl block. &self borrows the value to read it, &mut self borrows it to change it, and self takes ownership; functions without self, such as Player::new, are associated functions, often used as constructors.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)] generates standard trait implementations: Debug enables {:?} and the pretty {:#?}, Clone adds .clone(), and PartialEq adds == by comparing every field.
A tuple struct, such as struct Meters(f64), wraps values without naming them (height.0). It gives a plain number a type of its own, so metres can't be mixed up with seconds.
Inside an impl block, Self means the type being implemented, so fn new(name: &str) -> Self still reads correctly if the type is renamed.

lessons.title: Enums and pattern matching
objectives: Define enums whose variants carry data
Write exhaustive match expressions with ranges and guards
Use if let, let-else and matches!
key_points: An enum lists every form a value can take, and each variant can carry its own data: Circle { radius: f64 }, Rect { w: f64, h: f64 } or Triangle(f64, f64, f64). A value is always exactly one of the variants.

match compares a value with patterns and runs the first arm that fits. Patterns can destructure data (Shape::Rect { w, h }), match ranges (1..=9), add guards (x if x < 0) and catch everything else with _.
match must be exhaustive: an unhandled variant fails to compile with E0004, non-exhaustive patterns. So adding a variant to an enum shows you every match that needs updating.
if let Some(x) = value { ... } handles one pattern and ignores the rest. let Some(x) = value else { return; }, let-else, binds the value or leaves the function, which keeps the main path unindented.
match is an expression, so each arm produces a value, as in let label = match n { 0 => "zero", _ => "other" };. matches!(value, Pattern) gives a quick true or false.

lessons.title: Option and Result
objectives: Use Option for values that may be missing
Return and propagate errors with Result and ?
Write a custom error type that works with ? and Box<dyn Error>
key_points: Rust has no null: Option<T> is either Some(value) or None, and the compiler makes you handle both. Result<T, E> is either Ok(value) or Err(error), the standard return type for anything that can fail.
The ? operator unwraps an Ok or a Some, or returns the Err or None from the current function straight away. On a Result it also converts the error with From, so one error type can absorb another.
unwrap() and expect("message") panic on None or Err: fine in tests and experiments, risky in real code. Combinators such as map, and_then, unwrap_or and ok_or transform values without a match.

A custom error type is usually an enum with a variant per failure, implementing Display for its message and the std::error::Error trait; implementing From<ParseIntError> lets ? convert a library's error into it.
fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> lets main use ?. If main returns an Err, the program prints Error: followed by the error's Debug form, and exits with a failure status.

modules.title: Traits and generics
modules.summary: Share behaviour between types with traits, choose between static and dynamic dispatch, and write generic code with trait bounds, using the standard traits that make your types feel built in.

lessons.title: Traits
objectives: Define traits with required and default methods
Implement traits for your own types
Choose between impl Trait and dyn Trait
key_points: A trait defines behaviour as a set of method signatures, such as trait Summary { fn author(&self) -> String; }. A type implements it with impl Summary for Article { ... } and must provide every method that has no default.
A default method in the trait, such as summarise, works for every implementor through the required methods, and any implementor can override it with its own version.

fn notify(item: &impl Summary) accepts any type that implements the trait. The compiler makes a copy of the function for each type used (static dispatch), so the call costs no more than calling the method directly.

A trait object, such as Box<dyn Summary> or &dyn Summary, holds any implementing type behind a pointer, and finds the method at run time (dynamic dispatch). It's how one Vec holds different types that share a trait.
The orphan rule: you can implement a trait for a type only if the trait or the type is defined in your crate, so two crates can never provide conflicting implementations.

lessons.title: Generics and standard traits
objectives: Write generic functions and types with trait bounds
Implement standard traits such as Display, From and Add
Explain monomorphisation and associated types
key_points: Generics make code work for many types: fn largest<T: PartialOrd + Copy>(items: &[T]) -> Option<T> works for any T that can be compared and copied. Long bounds can move to a where clause.
Generic code is monomorphised: the compiler generates a specialised copy for each concrete type used, so generics cost nothing at run time, at the price of longer compiles and larger binaries.
Implement Display, fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result, for the text users see with {}, and derive Debug for the developer's view with {:?}.

From<T> defines a conversion, and implementing it gives you Into for free, so (3, 4).into() can build a Point. The operator traits in std::ops, such as Add, let your own types use + and the other operators.
Common derivable traits are Debug, Clone, Copy (cheap bitwise copies), PartialEq and Eq (==), PartialOrd and Ord (<, and sorting), Hash (for hash map keys) and Default (a zero value).
An associated type is a type that a trait leaves its implementors to choose, such as Iterator's Item or Add's Output, so each implementation names its own.

modules.title: Collections, closures and iterators
modules.summary: Work with Rust's collections (vectors, UTF-8 strings and hash maps), capture behaviour in closures, and process data with lazy iterator chains that compile to fast loops.

lessons.title: Vectors, strings and hash maps
objectives: Store and change data in a Vec<T>
Work with UTF-8 strings correctly
Count and group with HashMap and its entry API
key_points: Vec<T> is a growable array: push adds to the end and pop removes from it. v[i] panics if i is out of range, while v.get(i) returns an Option. Iterate with for x in &v to read and for x in &mut v to change the elements.

A String is UTF-8 text that owns its buffer, and s.len() counts bytes. Strings can't be indexed by a number (E0277), because a byte position may fall inside a character: use s.chars(), s.bytes() or slices on character boundaries.
HashMap<K, V> maps keys to values: insert adds or replaces, get returns an Option<&V>, and the entry API, *map.entry(key).or_insert(0) += 1, updates a value whether or not its key was there.
A HashMap's iteration order is unspecified. Use a BTreeMap when you need the keys in sorted order, and a HashSet or BTreeSet for a collection of unique values.
Collections own their contents: inserting a String into a map moves it in, and get gives back a reference. Use &str keys, or clone deliberately, when the caller needs to keep its data.

lessons.title: Closures
objectives: Write closures and pass them to functions
Explain how closures capture their environment
Tell Fn, FnMut and FnOnce apart
key_points: A closure is an anonymous function that can use variables from the place it's defined, as in let add = |x| x + n;. Its parameter and return types are usually inferred.

A closure captures each variable in the least demanding way it can: by shared reference to read it, by mutable reference to change it, or by value. move |x| ... forces capture by value, as needed when the closure outlives the variables.

Every closure implements one or more of three traits: Fn (only reads what it captured), FnMut (changes it) and FnOnce (consumes it, so it can be called only once). A function asks for the least it needs, as fn apply_twice<F: Fn(i32) -> i32> does.
Return a closure with impl Fn(i32) -> i32, as make_adder does. Each closure has its own unnamed type, so a function that can return different closures returns Box<dyn Fn(i32) -> i32>.
Closures make standard methods flexible: v.sort_by_key(|p| p.age), v.retain(|x| *x > 0) and the iterator adapters in the next lesson all take one.

lessons.title: Iterators
objectives: Chain iterator adapters and consumers
Collect results into collections
Implement Iterator for your own type
key_points: An iterator produces values one at a time through its next method, which returns Some(item) until it returns None. iter() yields references, iter_mut() mutable references and into_iter() owned values.

Adapters such as map, filter, enumerate, zip, skip, take and rev build a new iterator from another. They're lazy: nothing happens until a consumer, such as collect, sum, count, max, any or fold, asks for values.
collect() builds a collection from an iterator, and the target type decides which: Vec<_>, HashMap<_, _>, String, or even Result<Vec<_>, E>, which stops at the first error.
To make your own iterator, implement Iterator: name the type Item and write next. Every adapter and consumer then works with your type for free.

Iterator chains compile to code as fast as hand-written loops, a zero-cost abstraction, so use them where they read more clearly; a for loop is still the clearer choice when each step has side effects.

modules.title: Modules, testing and a command-line tool
modules.summary: Organise a Cargo package into a library, a binary and modules; test it with unit, integration and doc tests; and build a command-line tool that reads files, reports errors properly and ships as an optimised binary.

lessons.title: Modules, crates and Cargo
objectives: Split a package into a library, a binary and modules
Control visibility with pub, and paths with use
Add and manage dependencies with Cargo
key_points: A crate is what rustc compiles: a binary crate (src/main.rs) or a library crate (src/lib.rs). A package, described by Cargo.toml, holds at most one library and any number of binaries, and a binary uses the library by the package's name, as in use temps::Reading.

mod convert; in lib.rs declares a module whose code lives in src/convert.rs. Paths reach items through modules: crate::convert::c_to_f from the crate root, super:: for the parent module and self:: for the current one.

Items are private to their module unless marked pub, and using a private one elsewhere fails with E0603, function is private. A struct's fields need pub of their own, and pub use re-exports an item under a shorter path.

Dependencies go under [dependencies] in Cargo.toml, by hand or with cargo add name. A version such as "1.2" accepts any compatible 1.x release from 1.2 on, and Cargo.lock records the exact versions chosen.
Crates are published on crates.io and documented on docs.rs. Widely used ones include serde for serialisation, clap for command-line arguments and rand for random numbers.
cargo fmt formats every file with rustfmt, and cargo clippy runs Clippy's lints, which catch common mistakes and suggest more idiomatic code; both are worth running before every commit.

lessons.title: Testing
objectives: Write unit tests beside the code with #[test] and the assert macros
Add integration tests and doc tests
Run, filter and debug tests with cargo test and RustRover
key_points: A test is a function marked #[test], and it passes unless it panics. assert!(cond), assert_eq!(left, right) and assert_ne! panic with a helpful message; assert_eq! shows both values when they differ.

Unit tests usually live in a mod tests marked #[cfg(test)] at the bottom of the file they test, so they're compiled only by cargo test; use super::*; brings in the module's items, private ones included.
#[should_panic(expected = "no readings")] marks a test that passes only if the code panics with that message. A test can also return Result<(), E> and use ? instead of unwrap.

Integration tests live in the tests folder, each file its own crate that uses the library only through its public API. Doc tests are the ``` examples in /// comments, which cargo test compiles and runs, so documentation can't go stale.

cargo test builds and runs all three kinds, reporting each with a test result: ok. N passed line. cargo test name runs only the tests whose names contain name, and cargo test -- --nocapture shows the output of passing tests.

lessons.title: A command-line tool
objectives: Read command-line arguments and files
Report errors on standard error and set the exit code
Build an optimised release binary
key_points: std::env::args() yields the program's arguments as Strings, the first being the program's own path. Collect them into a Vec and match on a slice pattern, such as [path, column], to check how many there are.

std::fs::read_to_string(path) reads a whole file into a String and returns a Result whose io::Error explains failures, such as No such file or directory (os error 2); map_err adds context such as the file name.
Print results with println!, which goes to standard output, and problems with eprintln!, which goes to standard error, so output can be piped or redirected without error messages mixed in.
main can return std::process::ExitCode: ExitCode::SUCCESS (0), ExitCode::FAILURE (1) or ExitCode::from(2), so scripts can tell success from each kind of failure.
cargo run -- args passes everything after -- to the program. cargo build --release produces an optimised executable in target/release, ready to copy and run on its own.
For more than a couple of arguments, the clap crate parses options, generates --help text and reports usage errors, all from a struct definition with derive macros.

project.title: Build logstat, a log analyser
project.brief: Build logstat, a command-line tool that reads a service's log file and prints a summary: how many lines were well formed, which were malformed (by line number), how many lines there were at each level, which modules logged the most errors, latency statistics, and the time range covered. SPEC.md gives the exact line format, report format and exit codes, and expected-report.txt shows what a correct tool prints for the provided app.log, with and without --module payments. Structure it as a Cargo package with a library (parsing, aggregation and the report) and a thin binary. Model the log level as an enum that implements FromStr and Display, parse each line into a struct (borrowing from the line with a lifetime parameter, or owning its fields: your choice, explained), return a custom error enum for malformed lines, aggregate with iterators, closures and a HashMap, and give the report a Display implementation. Report problems on standard error with the right exit code. Test it with unit tests for parsing, integration tests that run the report on small samples, and at least one doc test, and keep it clean under cargo clippy and cargo fmt.
deliverables: A Cargo package with src/lib.rs (and modules if you like), a thin src/main.rs and Cargo.toml
Output identical to expected-report.txt for app.log, with and without --module payments
Unit tests for parsing (each kind of malformed line), integration tests in tests/, and at least one doc test, all passing
Exit status 1 for an unreadable file and 2 for bad usage, with a message on standard error
No warnings from cargo clippy --all-targets, and no changes from cargo fmt --check
A README explaining the design: the types, the error enum, where you borrowed or owned data, and why

rubric.name: Correct report
rubric.description: Matches expected-report.txt exactly for both runs, and handles an empty or wholly malformed file sensibly.

rubric.name: Types and errors
rubric.description: A level enum with FromStr and Display, a struct per entry, a custom error enum, and Result and ? throughout, with no unwrap on user input.

rubric.name: Ownership and lifetimes
rubric.description: Borrowing used where it avoids copying, lifetimes correct, and no needless clones.

rubric.name: Iterators and collections
rubric.description: Aggregation with iterator chains, closures and a HashMap or BTreeMap, in clear, idiomatic code.

rubric.name: Tests
rubric.description: Unit, integration and doc tests cover parsing, each malformed case, the percentiles and the module filter.

rubric.name: Tooling and README
rubric.description: Clippy and rustfmt clean, correct exit codes and messages on standard error, and a README that explains the design.

files.content:
# logstat: what the tool must do

Usage: logstat FILE [--module NAME]

## Well-formed lines

A line is well formed when it has, separated by single spaces:

1. a UTC timestamp such as 2026-03-14T09:00:30Z (YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ, with digits for the letters)
2. a level: DEBUG, INFO, WARN or ERROR
3. a module name in lower-case ASCII letters
4. a message of one or more words
5. last of all, latency_ms= followed by a whole number of milliseconds

Every other line is malformed: count it and report its line number (the first line is line 1).

## The report

    lines: <lines in the file>, parsed: <well formed>, malformed: <count> (lines <numbers, in order>)
    levels: DEBUG <n>, INFO <n>, WARN <n>, ERROR <n>
    errors by module: <the three modules with the most ERROR lines, most first, ties alphabetical>
    latency_ms: min <n>, median <n>, p95 <n>, max <n>
    time range: <first timestamp> to <last timestamp>

The time range uses the first and last well-formed lines, in file order. Percentiles use the
nearest-rank method: sort the latencies in ascending order; the p-th percentile is the value at
position ceil(p / 100 x count), counting from 1. The median is the 50th percentile.

With --module NAME, only that module's well-formed lines count towards the levels, errors,
latency and time range; the lines, parsed and malformed figures still describe the whole file.

## Exit codes

0 on success, 1 if the file can't be read, 2 for bad usage (no file, or an unknown option),
with a message on standard error for 1 and 2.

$ logstat app.log
lines: 120, parsed: 116, malformed: 4 (lines 17, 58, 93, 111)
levels: DEBUG 21, INFO 69, WARN 17, ERROR 9
errors by module: payments 6, auth 2, search 1
latency_ms: min 8, median 38, p95 141, max 950
time range: 2026-03-14T09:00:30Z to 2026-03-14T10:43:24Z

$ logstat app.log --module payments
